variants.title: Run one federated round
variants.context: One federated round has four owners: the coordinator selects an eligible cohort, clients train under a bounded contract, the aggregator recovers a valid aggregate after quorum, and the model owner evaluates before any release.
variants.prompt: A keyboard model trains across phones. Put the stages of one round in order, naming the owner of each.

items.text: Model owner: check global and cohort quality, privacy accounting, integrity canaries, and rollback criteria before canary.
Coordinator: filter for consent, model version, power and network policy, geography, and rate limits.
Aggregator: authenticate participants, reject incompatible schemas, and unmask only after the survivor threshold is met.
Client: verify the model and task, run bounded local work, clip the contribution, and report approved material only.

variants.hint: Which stage is the last one that can stop an unevaluated model from shipping?
variants.explanation: Each stage has a distinct owner and terminal outcome, so a retry cannot apply an update twice or promote a model that skipped its gates.

variants.title: Run one federated round
variants.context: One federated round has four owners: the coordinator selects an eligible cohort, clients train under a bounded contract, the aggregator recovers a valid aggregate after quorum, and the model owner evaluates before any release.
variants.prompt: Three hospitals join a cross-silo round with different schema versions. Put the stages in order for that round.

items.text: Aggregator: reject the site whose tensor schema does not match and aggregate the remaining valid updates.
Model owner: compare per-site quality and lineage before promoting the artifact to canary.
Client: each site loads local records, runs bounded training, and clips its update to the declared norm.
Coordinator: select the sites whose consent, jurisdiction, and model version match the round manifest.

variants.hint: Schema mismatch is caught by the stage that reads the update, not the stage that sent it.
variants.explanation: Validation belongs at the aggregator because only it sees every contribution against the frozen round manifest.

variants.title: Run one federated round
variants.context: One federated round has four owners: the coordinator selects an eligible cohort, clients train under a bounded contract, the aggregator recovers a valid aggregate after quorum, and the model owner evaluates before any release.
variants.prompt: Dropout during unmasking leaves the cohort one survivor short of the threshold. Put the stages in order for that round.

items.text: Aggregator: fail to reach the survivor threshold and record a typed abort instead of unmasking.
Model owner: release nothing, preserve the evidence, and record whether privacy budget was consumed.
Client: the accepted devices train locally and upload masked, clipped contributions.
Coordinator: invite the sampled cohort under the frozen eligibility policy and deadlines.

variants.hint: An aggregate that cannot be unmasked is a terminal state, not a partial result.
variants.explanation: Secure aggregation recovers only a threshold aggregate, so a short cohort ends in a typed abort with its evidence preserved.

variants.title: Size the round around survivors
variants.context: Invitations are not updates. Accepted equals invitations times observed availability, expected survivors equals accepted times one minus the dropout rate, and quorum margin equals expected survivors minus the required survivors.
variants.prompt: A round invites 900 devices, observed availability is 40 percent, and the dropout rate among accepted clients is 25 percent. How many survivors should the coordinator expect?
variants.hint: Two reductions apply in sequence, not one.
variants.explanation: Expected survivors equals invitations times availability times one minus dropout, so both funnel stages must be applied before quorum is judged.

mistakes.feedback: That stops at accepted clients and never applies the 25 percent dropout.
That treats invitations as updates, which ignores both availability and dropout.

variants.title: Size the round around survivors
variants.context: Invitations are not updates. Accepted equals invitations times observed availability, expected survivors equals accepted times one minus the dropout rate, and quorum margin equals expected survivors minus the required survivors.
variants.prompt: A round has 240 accepted clients and expects 15 percent dropout. The secure aggregation threshold requires 180 survivors. What is the quorum margin?
variants.hint: Margin is a subtraction after the dropout is applied.
variants.explanation: Quorum margin is expected survivors minus required survivors, and a thin margin means normal dropout variance can abort the round.

mistakes.feedback: That subtracts 180 from the 240 accepted clients without removing the expected dropout.
That is the expected dropout count, not the margin above the required survivors.

variants.title: Size the round around survivors
variants.context: Invitations are not updates. Accepted equals invitations times observed availability, expected survivors equals accepted times one minus the dropout rate, and quorum margin equals expected survivors minus the required survivors.
variants.prompt: A model is 200 MB and a compressed update is 35 percent of model size. The round has 500 accepted downloads and 300 surviving uploads. What is the round transfer in megabytes?
variants.hint: Downloads carry the model; uploads carry the compressed update.
variants.explanation: Round transfer is accepted downloads plus survivor uploads, so oversampling raises bytes and energy even when the extra clients never survive.

mistakes.feedback: That charges all 500 accepted clients an upload, but only the 300 survivors upload.
That counts only the downloads and drops the 21,000 megabytes of survivor uploads.

variants.title: Match the control to its boundary
variants.context: Layered controls protect different boundaries. Authenticated transport protects the network, secure aggregation hides individual updates from the coordinator, differential privacy bounds released information, and integrity controls handle malicious clients.
variants.prompt: A team lists its federated privacy controls. Match each control to the boundary it actually protects.

pairs.label: Authenticated transport
pairs.detail: The network boundary: traffic is encrypted, bound to a round and model version, and protected from replay.

pairs.label: Secure aggregation
pairs.detail: Coordinator visibility: only a threshold aggregate is recovered while individual surviving updates stay masked.

pairs.label: Differential privacy
pairs.detail: Released information: contributions are clipped, noise is calibrated, and privacy loss composes in an accountant.

pairs.label: Integrity controls
pairs.detail: Malicious participation: eligibility, attestation, rate limits, bounded influence, canaries, and rollback.

variants.hint: Ask who the attacker is in each case, not how strong the control sounds.
variants.explanation: The controls are complementary because each answers a different attacker, and none of them substitutes for the others.

variants.title: Match the control to its boundary
variants.context: Layered controls protect different boundaries. Authenticated transport protects the network, secure aggregation hides individual updates from the coordinator, differential privacy bounds released information, and integrity controls handle malicious clients.
variants.prompt: Four concerns are raised in a design review. Match each concern to the control that addresses it.

pairs.label: The coordinator itself should not see any one client's update
pairs.detail: Secure aggregation, which unmasks only after the survivor threshold.

pairs.label: Repeated releases could compose into a real leak over the lifetime
pairs.detail: Differential privacy with a trusted accountant over the declared scope.

pairs.label: A fabricated fleet of clients could steer the global model
pairs.detail: Integrity controls such as attestation, rate limits, and bounded influence.

pairs.label: A replayed message could resubmit last round's update
pairs.detail: Authenticated transport that binds messages to a round and model version.

variants.hint: One of these is a threat the coordinator poses rather than a threat it defends against.
variants.explanation: Transport does not hide updates from the coordinator, and differential privacy does not authenticate clients, so the mapping has to stay explicit.

variants.title: Match the control to its boundary
variants.context: Layered controls protect different boundaries. Authenticated transport protects the network, secure aggregation hides individual updates from the coordinator, differential privacy bounds released information, and integrity controls handle malicious clients.
variants.prompt: Controls interact in ways that must be resolved before launch. Match each stated cost to the control that causes it.

pairs.label: Server-side anomaly inspection of individual updates becomes impossible
pairs.detail: Secure aggregation, which is the control that hides them.

pairs.label: Small regressions on minority slices get harder to detect
pairs.detail: Differential privacy noise, which lowers sensitivity to small differences.

pairs.label: Abort risk rises whenever dropout is heavier than planned
pairs.detail: A high survivor threshold, chosen to enlarge the anonymity set.

pairs.label: New hardware, key management, and supply-chain dependencies appear
pairs.detail: Trusted execution and attestation added for integrity.

variants.hint: Every control buys a boundary and charges for it somewhere else.
variants.explanation: Control interactions are design decisions, so each protection is chosen with its operational cost named rather than assumed to be free.

variants.title: Recover from a failed round
variants.context: A failed round closes cleanly. Record a typed terminal reason, preserve immutable evidence, start a new round ID with clients resampled under current eligibility, and reuse no update unless protocol, consent, and privacy accounting allow it.
variants.prompt: The aggregator restarts after accepting some contributions but before producing an aggregate. Put the recovery steps in order.

items.text: Start a new round ID and resample clients under the current eligibility policy.
Alert on repeated aborts by cohort, because reliability failure can create selection bias.
Preserve the immutable evidence needed for audit and incident analysis.
Reuse no earlier update unless protocol, consent, and privacy accounting explicitly permit it.
Close the failed round with a typed terminal reason recording what was accepted.

variants.hint: Ambiguous material from a dead round is not a head start.
variants.explanation: Rounds close with typed reasons and fresh IDs so a restart cannot silently apply an update twice or reuse unaccounted material.

variants.title: Recover from a failed round
variants.context: A failed round closes cleanly. Record a typed terminal reason, preserve immutable evidence, start a new round ID with clients resampled under current eligibility, and reuse no update unless protocol, consent, and privacy accounting allow it.
variants.prompt: The evaluation service is unavailable after a release that already consumed privacy budget. Put the recovery steps in order.

items.text: Start a new round ID rather than retrying promotion against the same ambiguous bundle.
Record that the release consumed privacy budget, since exposure and promotion are separate questions.
Close the round with a terminal reason that names the failed evaluation gate.
Preserve the aggregate, accountant output, and lineage as immutable evidence.

variants.hint: Did anything get exposed, or did something merely fail to ship?
variants.explanation: Whether a failed release consumed budget depends on what was exposed, not on whether promotion succeeded.

variants.title: Recover from a failed round
variants.context: A failed round closes cleanly. Record a typed terminal reason, preserve immutable evidence, start a new round ID with clients resampled under current eligibility, and reuse no update unless protocol, consent, and privacy accounting allow it.
variants.prompt: One device class times out repeatedly and its rounds keep aborting. Put the recovery steps in order.

items.text: Alert on the repeated aborts by cohort instead of only on the aggregate abort rate.
Close each aborted round with the typed reason that identifies the timeout.
Preserve the participation funnel evidence for the affected cohort.
Resample under the current eligibility policy with the cohort's exclusion treated as a release risk.

variants.hint: A cohort that keeps failing is quietly leaving the training distribution.
variants.explanation: Repeated aborts by cohort are a selection-bias signal, so reliability failures are tracked per cohort rather than in aggregate.

variants.title: Judge the fit and the claim
variants.context: Federation adds orchestration, cryptography, unreliable participants, biased sampling, and distributed evaluation. It fits when raw data cannot move, enough participants clear quorum, and the privacy claim rests on more than data staying local.
variants.prompt: A team says its design is private because raw examples never leave the phone, and no clipping, noise, or accounting is planned. What is the accurate assessment?
options: Data placement is not a privacy guarantee, since updates can leak and repeated releases compose.
The design is private for user-level adjacency but still needs example-level accounting added.
The design is sound as long as transport is authenticated and credentials are rotated per round.
optionFeedback: Correct: federation is a data-placement architecture, and leakage, composition, and poisoning all survive it.
No adjacency claim holds without clipping, noise, and an accountant that matches the mechanism.
Transport protects the network path and leaves the coordinator's view of each update untouched.
variants.hint: Ask what an observer of the updates and releases can still learn.
variants.explanation: Keeping raw data local moves computation, and every update, aggregate, metric, and released model is still treated as sensitive.

variants.title: Judge the fit and the claim
variants.context: Federation adds orchestration, cryptography, unreliable participants, biased sampling, and distributed evaluation. It fits when raw data cannot move, enough participants clear quorum, and the privacy claim rests on more than data staying local.
variants.prompt: A poisoning canary regresses sharply while aggregate accuracy improves by half a point. What should the release gate do?
options: Promote the model and open an investigation, since the aggregate metric moved in the right direction.
Promote to a narrow canary so serving traffic can confirm whether the regression is real.
Block the release, because integrity evidence is an independent gate and not a weighted term.
optionFeedback: Aggregate accuracy cannot buy back a failed canary, because a backdoor is designed to leave the average intact.
A canary exposes users to a model whose integrity probe already failed, which inverts the purpose of the gate.
Correct: quality, population, privacy, and integrity gates are independent, so any one of them can stop a release.
variants.hint: Can a better average outvote a failed integrity probe?
variants.explanation: Federated release gates are independent, so a passing quality metric never compensates for failed integrity, privacy, or cohort evidence.

variants.title: Judge the fit and the claim
variants.context: Federation adds orchestration, cryptography, unreliable participants, biased sampling, and distributed evaluation. It fits when raw data cannot move, enough participants clear quorum, and the privacy claim rests on more than data staying local.
variants.prompt: Four regional business units already pool de-identified records under one policy that auditors accept, and they want to add federation. What is the better recommendation?
options: Adopt cross-device federation so each unit's records never leave its own regional store.
Adopt cross-silo federation so each unit can weight its contribution by its own record count.
Keep the centralized dataset, since it satisfies policy and gives better auditability here.
optionFeedback: Cross-device assumptions target many intermittent anonymous clients, which is not this population at all.
Cross-silo would fit if data could not move, but here it adds cryptography and sampling problems that are already solved.
Correct: federation is the weaker fit when a governed central dataset already satisfies policy and audits more simply.
variants.hint: Which constraint would federation actually be solving here?
variants.explanation: Federation earns its orchestration and cryptography only when the data-placement boundary solves a real constraint.
